chunks: Signal with and without preemphasis. The question: Draw the time-domain and frequency-domain spectrum of a signal with/without preemphasis.
Pre-emphasis changes a bit stream in a way you can see in two pictures. In the time picture, the first bit after a change stays at full height, but repeated bits are drawn lower.
In the frequency picture, the slow part of the signal is turned down while the fast part is left alone. The two pictures describe the same change.
A run of identical bits is slow, so lowering it lowers the slow part.
Think of the bass and treble knobs on a stereo. Slow, deep sounds are low frequency, and quick, sharp sounds are high frequency.
Pre-emphasis turns the bass down and leaves the treble alone. The song sounds brighter. Here, bass is the long runs of identical bits and treble is the edges where bits change.
A real driver has no knob, only weighted copies of the data.
The dashed grey trace is plain NRZ. The blue trace de-emphasizes: whenever a bit repeats (the 1 1 1 run and the 0 0 pairs), the level steps down to ±0. 5 after the first bit.
The transition levels are still ±1, so peak swing is unchanged and the driver doesn't clip.
The filter works by removing amplitude from the low-frequency bits, not by adding it to the edges.
Frequency: how fast something repeats. A long run of identical bits is slow, so it is low frequency. Spectrum: a chart of how much of the signal sits at each frequency.
NRZ: a bit stream with one fixed level per bit, high for 1 and low for 0. Transition: a bit that differs from the one before it.
De-emphasis: lowering repeated bits relative to transition bits ("Preemphasis: why and how").
Send the bits 0, 1, 1, 1, 0 as plain NRZ, with levels of minus 1 and +1. Now apply 6 decibels of de-emphasis (repeats drop to half height).
The first 1 follows a change, so it stays at 1. The next two 1 seconds are repeats, so they drop to 0. 5. The final 0 is a change, so it is back at minus 1.
The spectrum shows the same thing: the slow, low-frequency part falls by half in height, while an alternating 1010 pattern, which is all changes, is untouched.
That is the whole idea.
"Time domain: preemphasis keeps full swing on the first bit after a transition and lowers the following repeated bits, a shoulder after each edge.
Frequency domain: the NRZ sinc-squared spectrum is multiplied by a high-pass shape, so DC drops by 6 decibels while the Nyquist region stays put.
Since the channel is a low-pass, the two combine to a flatter overall response, and at the receiver the isolated bits and long runs reach more similar levels, which opens the eye."
